https://www.politico.eu/article/good-bad.text: BRUSSELS — Bulgaria’s looming multimillion-euro fine stole the show Tuesday when the European Commission unveiled its report cards for EU governments over their public spending. The report cards present a gloomy picture of EU public finances, as many governments face the challenge of repairing deteriorating finances amid global trade tensions, war, skyrocketing energy prices and rising borrowing costs. So far, the bloc’s economy has proven resilient to outside shocks and is forecast to grow by 1.4% this year and next . That resilience won’t last forever. “Absorbing temporary shocks is not the same as adapting to permanent change,” such as artificial intelligence and higher interest rates, Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis said ahead of Brussels’ latest round of economic oversight, known as the European Semester . “The European economy must go beyond resilience towards real dynamism, and that will be essential to secure our prosperity and social model.” Advertisement Advertisement Sofia is the only capital facing a cash fine for failing to rein in its spending. But there are plenty of other countries that have broken the fiscal rules, which are designed to keep the gap between government spending and what they collect in revenue to 3% of economic output. They also aim to keep public debt-to-GDP ratios below 60%. Brussels currently has red flags pinned in 10 countries, including France, Belgium and Italy, to signal to investors which governments have fallen foul of the EU rules. Countries shed the undesirable labels once they convince Brussels that their spending is under control. But the Commission has allowed for extra budgetary leeway for 19 countries to build up their militaries in an effort to deter further Russian aggression. These are POLITICO’s grades, weighing countries’ fiscal outlooks alongside Brussels’ findings. Bulgaria and Hungary: F Budapest and Sofia have strayed so far from their spending commitments that Brussels is prepared to punish them. Both governments could lose access to some EU funds, while Bulgaria faces a fine of up to €23 million. Even after allowing extra leeway for defense spending, Hungary’s spending overshoot is estimated at 3.1% of GDP this year, and Bulgaria’s at 2.3%. Only eurozone countries can be fined, sparing Hungary that particular punishment. Belgium and France: E Passing on paper is one thing. Delivering is another. France has produced a draft budget for next year, but its government is struggling to get it through the National Assembly. Belgium’s five-party coalition, meanwhile, can’t agree on its spending plans . Advertisement Advertisement The Commission has given both the benefit of the doubt. It rubber-stamped France’s draft budget, while flagging uncertainty over the parliamentary debate. Without Belgium’s plans, the EU executive relied on its economic forecast, which projects spending within the rules. Both countries nevertheless have deficits above 5% of GDP and debt exceeding 110% of economic output. The Commission will check their progress again in the spring. Spain and Germany: D Spain’s deficit remains below 3% of GDP and its economy is forecast to grow by more than 2% this year and next. Spanish debt is also set to fall by 2 percentage points to 97.2% of GDP over the next two years. Turns out that isn’t good enough for Brussels, which had harsh words for Madrid. Spanish spending is growing faster than it promised, even after Brussels granted Spain more budgetary flexibility to build up its defenses. As for Germany, the Commission warned that its spending plans risk falling foul of the rules — but stopped short of slapping a red flag on its budget. Europe’s largest economy is expected to keep its debt level below 70% of GDP, but its budget deficit is projected to climb from 4.1% this year to 4.5% in 2028. Extra leeway for defense spending doesn’t fully explain the deficit overshoot. But Brussels held off because the remaining excess is small and the estimates uncertain. “One could say that, indeed, Germany was a close call from that point of view,” Dombrovskis said.
